sources.title: Screaming in the Cloud: Coding Agents, Chaos, and the Future of Dev Work
Qodo Agentic Review: Closing the gap: AI agent hype and production reality

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: people are going way too far on the, like throw more tokens at the problem
cards.claim: Throwing more tokens at a problem works only when the problem is verifiable; it is over-applied to problems that are not.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument from the Ralph/compiler example; no numbers.
cards.landing: Effort routing and verifier design: spend tokens only where a deterministic check exists

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you can create good deterministic back pressure
cards.claim: More tokens help when you can build good deterministic backpressure; a programming language is infinitely verifiable (compile, run, fix), so the model can check its own work.
cards.evidence_detail: Ralph Wiggum language-building example; no numbers.
cards.landing: CI gates and verification scripts as backpressure; phase routine should name the deterministic check per task

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think one of my predictions is by the end of 2026, most agents are gonna remove the Bash tool
cards.claim: Prediction: by end of 2026 most agents will drop the general Bash tool for narrower scoped tools or a minimal bash-like thing, for safety, security and reliability.
cards.evidence_detail: Prediction; he notes the MCP context-clutter complaint holds only if a Bash tool exists.
cards.landing: Tool permissions / allowlists in .claude settings; narrow scoped tools or agents

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we tried the, like don't read the code thing for about six months
cards.claim: His team tried not reading code for about six months, then ran from it and threw out the whole codebase (frontend and backend tangled) to restart greenfield.
cards.evidence_detail: Own team experience; codebase discarded.
cards.landing: Owner/reviewer reading of code in the phase routine; argues against fully hands-off phases

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I have a little journal of things that AI is not good at solving
cards.claim: Keep a personal journal of problems AI failed at and re-run them as evals on each new model or workflow.
cards.evidence_detail: Example: a cross-component race condition he tests every new model against for about six months.
cards.landing: A standing set of hard-case evals to re-run when changing model or effort level; decisions journal

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you improve the factory 10%, well, you get, you know, 20% of your time back
cards.claim: Investing in the software factory (sandboxes, CI/CD, automated testing) gives compounding returns, a point past which you leave others behind.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers from experience, no measurement.
cards.landing: Justifies saving workflows and agents as reusable factory assets

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you put a human in here, it is high leverage for a human to read it
cards.claim: Build workflows that put humans at high-leverage points, e.g. reviewing a 200-line markdown summary of a change at the 25,000-foot level before 1000-2000 lines of code are written.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as principle; the same ratio appears in the Qodo episode.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha PR body and owner one-page view as the human review point

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the quadratic nature of a attention and the like increasing cost and decreasing quality
cards.claim: The durable, model-independent skill is understanding attention: quality falls and cost rises as the context window fills, so context management stays relevant across model generations.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual argument; no numbers.
cards.landing: Basis for one-phase-per-session and for trimming always-loaded CLAUDE.md

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: learn how to push those models 10 to 15% further on specific tasks
cards.claim: Harness and workflow customisation gets 10-15% (maybe 50%) better results on a specific task and the skill carries across models even when custom code is obsoleted by the next model.
cards.evidence_detail: Estimated range, not measured; framed against the bitter lesson.
cards.landing: Argues that per-task workflow scripts are disposable but the understanding is kept; relevant to what to save

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you start with three prompts and then you wake up the next day and suddenly you have a hundred
cards.claim: Engineers glue agent systems together and prompts sprawl until only the author can use them (people reinventing Gastown).
cards.evidence_detail: Observation of many practitioners.
cards.landing: Warning about uncurated skill/prompt sprawl as skills are added

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Nobody owes you cheap inference.
cards.claim: Serious enterprise customers pay per token anyway; do not plan around subsidized flat-rate inference.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated from enterprise customer experience.
cards.landing: Cost-aware effort routing (verifier effort level, model choice)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: most of the vertical AI shipped to enterprise is ignoring the bitter lesson
cards.claim: Teams actually delivering vertical AI results build specific prompts, pipelines and workflows for today's models rather than waiting for the models to improve; there will always be a jagged frontier.
cards.evidence_detail: Paraphrased from transcript ("They're all ignoring the bidder lesson"); no data.
cards.landing: Supports investing in a reusable workflow library despite model churn

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: they will make a big mess
cards.claim: Models are good at some things but not codebase architecture; left unattended they make a mess, and the industry cycles from 'stop reading code' back to reading it about every five months.
cards.evidence_detail: His team: stopped reading code in August, reverted around Nov/Dec after about 5 months, rebuilt most of the product.
cards.landing: Human architecture review gate in phase routine; do not drop code reading

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't ask a model on a scale of one to 100, how good is this PR?
cards.claim: Use models for binary classifications (has unit tests? do they cover the thing that matters?) and compute the score deterministically yourself; never ask for a holistic score.
cards.evidence_detail: Design principle for code review bots; no numbers.
cards.landing: Reviewer prompt design: per-register-id yes/no questions with a deterministic roll-up instead of an Opus holistic verdict

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't leak the understanding of what is good or bad into the model
cards.claim: Do not leak what you want to hear into the reviewing model, because it will tell you what you want to hear; keep the reviewer independent of the desired answer.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning about sycophancy; the hosts agree models follow instructions.
cards.landing: Refuter prompts that avoid stating the author's expected conclusion; supports refuted-by-default, fresh context

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's very easy to accidentally, like, have AI for code review be kind of useless
cards.claim: Naive AI code review is useless: asked to find problems it lists about 30 issues, asked if the PR is good it approves; the models are too easily oversteered.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience, no measurement.
cards.landing: Opus reviewer per PR; guard against prompt framing that determines the verdict

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: reading 100 or 200 lines of Markdown, and that at least grounds me
cards.claim: A good review bot explains the PR by compressing thousands of lines into 100-200 lines of markdown so the human knows which parts to check.
cards.evidence_detail: Seen in review bots; no numbers.
cards.landing: Owner one-page view and PR body summary

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you actually don't have too many PRs. What you have is too many bad PRs.
cards.claim: The review bottleneck is bad PRs, not PR volume; AI-era PRs usually need 50% or more rework, and perfect PRs are a joy to review.
cards.evidence_detail: Says rework is 'usually more like 50% or more' without data.
cards.landing: Put quality upstream of review (plan/design) rather than adding review volume

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: most of the PRs that come through need less than 5% rework
cards.claim: Upstream alignment on a roughly 200-line markdown design doc (after research, before plan) for a 2,000-line change brings PR rework under 5%, versus 50% typical.
cards.evidence_detail: Team of three; rework figures are stated, not measured; show notes say 50% to under 5%.
cards.landing: Design-doc step between research and plan in the phase routine; Plan @ sha PR

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're just shifting the bottleneck to some other place
cards.claim: A Linear-ticket software factory with research/plan review stages just converted 40 to-do tickets into 40 tickets in research and review; the bottleneck moved rather than disappeared.
cards.evidence_detail: Internal experiment from about September; no timings.
cards.landing: Owner review capacity as the limiting resource; limit the number of concurrent phases

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Any specification that takes the same amount to read as the code itself, just read the code.
cards.claim: A spec only has leverage at roughly 20% compression of the code; a 1,000-line line-by-line plan drifted about 20% from the final code, so it was not worth reviewing.
cards.evidence_detail: Plan files of about 1000 lines; end code differed about 20% from plan.
cards.landing: Keep plan documents short and decision-level; avoid line-by-line plans in the phase routine

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I hate the word spec
cards.claim: He avoids the word 'spec' because it is semantically diffuse (PRD, detailed PRD, code in English); name the artifact by its level of detail.
cards.evidence_detail: Terminology argument.
cards.landing: Precise artifact names in CLAUDE.md and phase routine (plan, design doc, register)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the smaller you can make those tool cycles, the more you can break down
cards.claim: Split a broad agent into a classifier handing off to specialised agents with about 30 tools each; this is more brittle but solves the specific tasks better, a trade-off.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers (20 agents, 30 tools).
cards.landing: Narrow custom agents and sub-agents beside the Haiku locator

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every token in is the only thing that influences
cards.claim: Context engineering means deciding deterministically what goes into each single LLM call; the tokens in are the only control over the quality of tokens out, including at turn 50.
cards.evidence_detail: Definition.
cards.landing: Basis for trimming CLAUDE.md and deciding what loads per phase

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the model who is doing the conversation has no way to modify its own memory
cards.claim: Good memory systems are deterministic: a separate model in a separate context compacts conversations into decaying-resolution summaries (14 days, weekly, monthly) that are injected without the working model editing them.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes implementations he has seen.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store design: a separate writer step and deterministic injection, not agent-chosen recall

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're going to end up building it yourself
cards.claim: Off-the-shelf memory systems or agent harnesses get you to 80% quickly; at the wall you reverse engineer them and end up building your own, and high-quality products engineer every token.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion from observed products.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store pilot: build the primitives in-house rather than adopt a memory product

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: split your workflow up into smaller sessions to get better results
cards.claim: Splitting the workflow into smaller sessions raises the ceiling on the hardest solvable problem, and the RPI system had to be adapted from power users to average users.
cards.evidence_detail: Rolled RPI out to companies from startups to Fortune 500 over 2-4 months.
cards.landing: Supports one phase per new session; note that a routine must survive average-user use

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I would rather have him tear apart a 200-line Markdown doc
cards.claim: Seek review of the design doc before the code is written, because changes are cheap before the author is attached to polished, test-passing code.
cards.evidence_detail: His practice with CTO Kyle; design review optional in a three-person team.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha draft PR reviewed before implementation begins

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a benchmark for, like, a long-term code maintainability
cards.claim: Planned benchmark: a model implements 20 features without seeing the roadmap, then a smaller model implements the 21st, to measure whether code gets worse over time (not one-off PR reproduction).
cards.evidence_detail: Work in progress; no results given (later report is SlopCodeBench).
cards.landing: Possible measure of architecture quality across phases; precursor of SlopCodeBench

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: hard to, like, evaluate deterministically in a, like, reinforcement learning gym
cards.claim: Models cannot be RL-trained on architecture because 'is it well designed' has no deterministic check beyond asking another model; he sees no path to models being good at architecture, so bake opinions into skills.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned claim.
cards.landing: Keep human architecture review; encode architecture opinions as skills and import-linter contracts

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Generating low-quality code is nearly free; defending against it is expensive
cards.claim: The war on slop is asymmetric: producing bad code is free while defending against it costs far more (OpenCode and Pydantic drowning in bot PRs).
cards.evidence_detail: Attributed to a Swyx talk framing; examples are projects drowning in PRs.
cards.landing: Argues review capacity rather than generation is the constraint; cap outputs

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: your job is now to wear the senior engineering hat
cards.claim: In the AI era the junior's job is to make the system safer (guardrails) so the model just goes; accumulated senior taste should be captured and applied at design time, which is worth more than at review.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; cites Mario Zechner on embracing friction.
cards.landing: Encode owner taste as skills, rules and contracts used at design time

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Shipping is, like, getting it deployed, testing it, monitoring it in production
cards.claim: Shipping differs from coding; feedback loops wiring support queue, Sentry and Datadog back to a model can be automated but architecture still needs a human.
cards.evidence_detail: Credits Guillermo Rauch for the framing.
cards.landing: Production feedback loop (Sentry) as a verifier input for post-deploy phases

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 4.5, I actually think, is not as smart a model as Opus 4.1
cards.claim: His view that Opus 4.5 was less smart than Opus 4.1 but faster, cheaper and better for people who did not know what they were doing.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal opinion; no benchmark.
cards.landing: Model-choice per task: capability is not monotonic with version number; test before assuming

gaps: Both transcripts are on-page text; the Qodo transcript was lightly mangled by apostrophe loss only. The Screaming in the Cloud audio and any hidden timestamps were not checked.
Bitter-lesson quote in R21-12 is paraphrased from an auto-caption typo, so no verbatim quote was used.
